segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the Spirit says explicitly that in later times some will fall away from the faith, devoting themselves to deceiving spirits and teachings of demons

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: through the hypocrisy of liars whose own conscience has been seared,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who forbid marriage and demand abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and have come to know the truth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For everything God created is good, and nothing is to be rejected when it is received with thanksgiving,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for it is made holy through the word of God and prayer.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If you put these things before the brothers and sisters, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, nourished on the words of the faith and of the good teaching that you have followed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But have nothing to do with profane old wives’ tales. Train yourself instead for godliness;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for physical training is beneficial to a small extent, but godliness is beneficial in every way, since it holds a promise of life, both the present life and the life to come.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The saying is trustworthy and deserves full acceptance,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for this is why we labor and are insulted: because we have set our hope on the living God, who is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Command these things and teach them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let no one look down on you for being young, but become an example for the believers in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading, to exhortation, to teaching.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy with the laying on of hands by the council of elders.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Practice these things; be immersed in them, so that your progress may be plain to everyone.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Keep watch on yourself and on the teaching. Persist in these things, for by doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you.

notes.note: The verb means to burn with a hot iron. It can picture a conscience cauterized into numbness, as rendered here, or a conscience “branded,” as slaves and criminals were, with a mark of ownership (here, by the demonic powers of verse 1). Both readings have scholarly support, and the Greek does not decide between them.

Most translations have “sanctified” or “consecrated.” The Greek verb is built on the ordinary word for “holy,” and “made holy” keeps that link audible. The meaning is not in dispute; the point is that food received with thanks belongs within the sphere of what is God’s, against those who declare it off limits.

notes.phrase: the word of God and prayer
notes.traditional: the word of God and prayer
notes.note: What “the word of God” refers to is debated. It may be God’s declaration in Genesis that what he made is good, scriptural phrases used in thanksgiving at meals, or the gospel message. The second noun is a word for petition or prayer addressed to God, here evidently the thanksgiving said over food.

The Greek plural is grammatically masculine but was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women, here the whole community of believers. “Brothers” alone would suggest to a modern reader that only men are meant. Many recent translations make the same choice.

Literally “myths of the kind old women tell.” This was a stock expression of contempt in ancient philosophical debate for stories considered unworthy of serious attention. It dismisses the opponents’ teaching and is not a comment on older women as such.

The Greek phrase is literally “for a little” and can mean either “to a limited degree” or “for a short time.” The contrast with “in every way” favors the first, but the reference to the present life and the life to come gives the second some support.

This adjective is normally rendered “faithful” or “believing” in this translation. Applied to a saying it means reliable or worthy of trust, and “a faithful saying” would now suggest a statement that accurately reproduces some original, so “trustworthy” is used for this formula.

This formula occurs five times in the letters to Timothy and Titus. Here it is unclear whether it points back to the statement about godliness in verse 8 or forward to verse 10. Most interpreters take it with verse 8, but the question is open.

Manuscripts are divided between “we are insulted” (the reading of the Greek text translated here, and of the King James tradition) and “we struggle,” which differs by a few letters and is followed by many modern translations. Both readings are ancient and editors disagree about which is original.

The usual meaning of the word is “especially,” which makes God the Savior of all people in some sense and of believers in a fuller one. Some scholars argue that it can mean “that is to say,” which would limit the statement to believers. That sense is disputed and is not adopted here.

The noun refers to reading aloud to a gathering, not private study. In synagogue and church the Scriptures were read out to the assembled community, most of whom did not own or could not read books, and the reading was followed by exhortation and teaching, the two activities named next.

candidates.reason: Key term of the Pastoral Epistles, Acts and 2 Peter that translators render variously as godliness, piety, devotion or reverence; readers need one word to follow the theme.
The plural for mixed groups of believers occurs across the whole New Testament and needs one policy on brothers versus brothers and sisters.
Ranges over exhortation, encouragement and comfort across Acts, Paul and Hebrews, and needs a sense-by-sense decision to avoid random variation.
Recurs in Romans, 1 Corinthians, the Pastorals and 1 Peter; translators vary between gift, spiritual gift and grace-gift, and the link with χάρις needs a consistent policy.
Very frequent in the Pastorals and traditionally split between doctrine and teaching; one rendering should hold throughout.
